Ourscamp
OORS-kahn
n. (a Cistercian abbey on the Oise, founded 1129 as a daughter of Clairvaux; its infirmary hall survives and is known as the hall of the dead)
French ours, a bear, and camp, a field: the bear's field, from a local legend attached to the site.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Ourscamp was founded in 1129 beside the Oise in Picardy, a daughter of Clairvaux, and became a large and wealthy house. What survives is unusual: the roofless Gothic choir of the church stands as a shell, and beside it the thirteenth-century infirmary hall, long called the salle des morts — the hall of the dead — where the sick of the house were nursed and where they died. The building is intact and still in religious use. An abbey that kept a named room for dying in was doing something the modern world has arranged not to do, and Scripture is on the abbey's side. “And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27) is stated as a plain appointment; “So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom” (Psa 90:12) makes the counting of them a prayer; and “LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is; that I may know how frail I am” (Psa 39:4) asks to be told. A house with a hall of the dead in daily view had its theology of mortality built into its floor plan.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines infirmary as a lodging for the sick, a hospital; mortality as subjection to death or the necessity of dying, and also death; and die as to be deprived of respiration, of the circulation of blood, and other bodily functions.

expand to see more

INFIRMARY, n. A lodging for the sick; a hospital, or place where the sick and infirm are received and nursed.

MORTALITY, n. Subjection to death, or the necessity of dying; also, death; and frequency of death.

DIE, v.i. To be deprived of respiration, of the circulation of blood, and other bodily functions, and rendered incapable of resuscitation.

FRAIL, a. Weak; infirm; liable to fail and decay; subject to casualties; easily destroyed.

NUMBER, v.t. To count; to reckon; to ascertain the units of any sum, collection or multitude.

Key Scripture

Heb 9:27 — "And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:"

Psa 90:12 — "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."

Psa 39:4 — "LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is; that I may know how frail I am."

Job 14:1 — "Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble."

Modern Corruption

A Picardy abbey of 1129 whose surviving infirmary is still called the hall of the dead: a house with its theology of mortality built into the floor plan.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the numbering of days as a discipline. “that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom” (Psa 90:12) ties the counting to the wisdom — a man who will not think about dying will not think clearly about living either.

The live corruption is the modern management of death out of sight, into institutions designed so that most people never see it. That is a change in architecture before it is a change in doctrine, and it has made “Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble” (Job 14:1) sound like pessimism rather than observation. A hall of the dead at the heart of a house is the opposite arrangement, and the honester one.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew maveth (H4194), death; Hebrew yom (H3117), a day; Greek thanatos (G2288), death; Greek hapax (G530), once; Hebrew chadel (H2310), frail or transient.

expand to see more

Hebrew maveth (H4194) — death; in the Old Testament an enemy, never a friend.

Hebrew yom (H3117) — a day; “So teach us to number our days” (Psa 90:12).

Greek thanatos (G2288) — death; the last enemy, and a defeated one.

Greek hapax (G530) — once, once for all; “as it is appointed unto men once to die” (Heb 9:27).

Hebrew chadel (H2310) — frail, transient; “that I may know how frail I am” (Psa 39:4).

Usage

"“but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27) — the clause that makes the hall of the dead a serious room."

"“the measure of my days, what it is” (Psa 39:4) — a prayer to be told the truth about oneself."

"“is of few days, and full of trouble” (Job 14:1) — observation rather than gloom."
